extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers and educators (especially children's/middle-grade authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical standards for writing middle-grade/children's novels (particularly fantasy) including storytelling craft, audience-appropriate content, representation of learning differences, revision/testing with target readers, and steps toward publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat kids like intelligent readers / don't 'write down' to them
rubrics_metrics.description: I didn’t simplify anything to write The Lightning Thief. I didn’t worry about vocabulary or sentence length or book length... I think it would be a mistake to 'write down' to kids. They hate that. They want to be treated like intelligent and sophisticated readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not artificially simplify language, sentence structure, or style solely because the audience is young. Maintain strong prose and respect readers' intelligence while ensuring content is age-appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast-paced storytelling / keep readers asking questions
rubrics_metrics.description: I think kids want the same thing from a book that adults want — a fast-paced story... A good book always keeps you asking questions, and makes you keep turning pages so you can find out the answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the narrative to sustain momentum and curiosity: clear plot, cliffhangers, and pacing that avoids long, digressive passages. Make each scene propel the reader forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long descriptions / tighten storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Kids get bored with long descriptions that go on for pages and pages. They get bored with books that don’t seem to have a clear plot... writing a children’s book made me a better adult writer, because I forced myself to tighten up my storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut or condense extended descriptive passages; prioritize scenes that develop plot or character. Tighten prose to maintain engagement across age groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create characters worth caring about
rubrics_metrics.description: I think kids want the same thing from a book that adults want — ... characters worth caring about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop protagonists and supporting characters with clear desires, flaws, and growth so readers can form emotional investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humor, surprises, and mystery to engage
rubrics_metrics.description: I think kids want the same thing from a book that adults want — ... humor, surprises and mystery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer humor and unexpected developments into plot and dialogue; use mystery to sustain curiosity and reward readers with satisfying reveals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make content age-appropriate; be transparent to parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Are your adult mysteries appropriate for young readers? No, they’re not designed for kids... I do not recommend them for readers under 17. As with any book, I would encourage parents to read Percy Jackson and decide for themselves whether it’s right for their children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of sexual content, language, and adult situations when writing for younger readers; provide clear guidance for parents and guardians and err on the side of appropriateness for the target age bracket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray learning differences respectfully and as strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: I was surprised to learn that ADHD and dyslexia frequently go together... dyslexic/ADHD kids are creative, 'outside-the-box' thinkers... Making Percy ADHD/dyslexic was my way of honoring the potential of all the kids I’ve known who have those conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research conditions (read reputable books and sources), avoid stereotyping, and present learning differences honestly while emphasizing strengths and potential rather than deficits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do research when depicting sensitive topics
rubrics_metrics.description: While this was happening, I did a lot of reading about dyslexia and ADHD. I especially liked the books Keeping a Head in School and Driven to Distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult authoritative resources and, when possible, people with lived experience to ensure accurate, empathetic, and informed representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show early drafts to target readers (audience testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: I picked a few of my sixth, seventh and eighth graders and asked them if they’d be willing to 'test drive' the novel... The kids really liked it. They had some good suggestions, too. They helped me pick the best title for the book. They also had some good ideas on how Percy should act if he had ADHD... One student helped me refine the way Percy’s sword... worked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feedback from actual members of your target age group to evaluate engagement, character behavior, title appeal, and plausibility of details; iterate based on concrete suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on story first, not preaching; let themes emerge
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t consciously put messages in the books, because my job is telling a good story, not preaching. However, I do pick up on themes from Greek mythology that still resonate... man’s relationship to nature is one of those.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize compelling storytelling; allow thematic material to arise naturally rather than inserting overt moralizing. Readers will derive meaning from strong narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find what you MUST write (follow compulsions/passions)
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to find what you MUST write. When you find it, you will know, because the subject matter won’t let you go. It’s not enough to write simply because you think it would be neat to be published. You have to be compelled to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose projects that feel essential to you, where the idea persists until you complete it; intrinsic motivation produces stronger work than chasing publication alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write every day and keep practicing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write every day! Keep a journal. Jot down interesting stories you heard. Write descriptions of people you see... Writing is like a sport — you only get better if you practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish regular writing habits, maintain a journal, and treat consistent practice as the primary route to improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely to learn craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Read a lot! Read everything you can get your hands on. You will learn the craft of writing by immersing yourself in the voices, styles, and structures of writers who have gone before you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study diverse authors and genres to absorb techniques, narrative strategies, and stylistic variations; active reading is a form of craft training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a mentor and don't be afraid to ask for help
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing a young writer needs is a mentor who believes in his or her talent. So don’t be afraid to ask for help! Find a teacher you respect. Correspond with authors. You will find that a polite email will often get a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek teachers, peers, or published authors for feedback and guidance; polite outreach can open doors and provide encouragement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in a line edit / use endorsements in queries
rubrics_metrics.description: A Bay Area creative writing teacher/author had done a line edit for me. She really helped me clean up the final draft, and then let me use her name in my query letter... For this reason, I do think it can be helpful to pay someone for a line edit, if you have someone reputable in your area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider paying a reputable editor for a line edit to improve manuscript quality and potentially gain a named endorsement to strengthen agent queries. Look for freelance editors via writing institutes and colleges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect rejection; be persistent with agents and publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Once I had a completed manuscript, I queried agents. Many said no. One said yes... Many publishers said no, all for different reasons... Finally, however, we got an offer... The time from first query letter to pub date took three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate multiple rejections and variable feedback; persist in querying, revising, and shopping the manuscript until you find the right match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your real experience and students as inspiration, but be mindful
rubrics_metrics.description: I frequently used names of former students for my characters, but the kids were always surprised how long it took to get a name into print... Percy is also based on many students I have taught in the past, and partly on my son’s own struggle with ADHD/dyslexia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on teaching and life experience for authentic detail, but be aware of privacy/timing and fictionalize appropriately; consider the ethical implications of using real people as templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize potentially controversial content within cultural/literary tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: These stories are part of our collective heritage... If censors want to challenge Percy Jackson on the grounds that it portrays the Greek gods as real, they’ll have to censor a good portion of the English curriculum... Greek mythology is studied extensively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting myth/religion, emphasize literary and educational context to defuse censorship concerns; present material as part of cultural heritage rather than as an attack on beliefs.
